intro: Jerusalem artichokes are not true artichokes at all, but vigorous sunflower relatives grown for their knobbly underground tubers. They are hardy, reliable and useful for winter soups, stews and grated salads, with a sweet, nutty flavour which is not to everybody's taste and may not suit every digestion. The plants grow very tall in rich soil, making them useful as a screen or windbreak but also capable of robbing light from lower crops if planted in a long row. They are easy to grow from tubers, but hard to eradicate once established because even small pieces left in the soil can regrow.

Globe artichoke is a large, handsome thistle-family perennial grown for its unopened flower buds, not for underground tubers and not related to Jerusalem or Chinese artichokes. It is decorative enough for a border, with grey-green fern-like leaves and strong stems, but it needs more space than most vegetables and is not a natural choice for a very small garden. The reward is a distinctive, nutty crop: pick the heads while they are still tight, green and tender, before the scales open and the centre becomes tough. The plants establish quickly in rich, moist but well-drained soil, though they need regular watering, feeding, mulching and some protection in cold winters.

Aubergines are decorative, heat-loving relatives of the tomato, grown for their glossy fruits as well as their purple flowers and large velvety leaves. They can crop well under glass or in a warm polytunnel, but outdoors they are a gamble except in very warm, sheltered places. The key requirement is heat: cool, grey weather slows growth and often delays fruiting until late summer. Treat aubergines as tender annuals, give them rich soil, steady moisture without waterlogging, and harvest the fruits while the skin still has its shine. Fruits may be oval, round or long, and varieties range from the familiar dark purple to white, violet and striped forms.

Leaf beets are a useful answer for gardeners who like spinach but find true spinach quick to bolt or difficult in dry weather. Swiss chard, seakale beet, spinach beet and perpetual spinach are all grown for leaves rather than swollen roots, and a few plants can provide many pickings over a long season. Swiss chard has broad leaves with thick, edible midribs, often white but sometimes red, yellow or pink, and it is ornamental enough for the flower border. Spinach beet has a plainer green leaf, tastes similar to spinach but is generally more acidic and contains less oxalic acid than true spinach. The main rule is to pick regularly: small leaves are tender and useful for salads or cooking, while over-large leaves become tougher and the plant slows down.

Capsicums include both sweet peppers and chillies: colourful, heat-loving members of the tomato and potato family. In their native climate they are perennial plants, but in Britain they are grown as tender annuals and are most reliable under glass or in a warm, sheltered position. Green peppers are edible but are still an immature stage; if left to ripen they change colour and, in many varieties, become sweeter or hotter and more deeply flavoured. That extra flavour comes at a cost, because ripe-coloured fruit take longer to develop and the plant produces fewer new peppers while they mature. The crop is therefore a balance between earlier, heavier green harvests and later, smaller harvests of fully coloured fruit.

Celeriac, or turnip-rooted celery, is grown for its swollen stem-base rather than for crisp stalks. It brings a strong earthy celery flavour to soups, stews, salads and winter dishes, and stores well into spring if lifted and kept cool. Although it avoids much of the blanching and earthing-up work of celery, it is still a long-season crop that needs rich, moisture-retentive soil, steady watering in dry weather and a good start under cover. The roots are fibrous and shallow, so growth is checked badly on dry ground; heavy, well-composted soil suits it especially well. Most varieties are quite similar, but all need the whole season to make a good-sized root.

Chicory is grown in two useful ways: for green salad leaves in summer and autumn, and for pale, crisp chicons forced indoors to give fresh winter salad. The flavour is refreshing, tart and sometimes bitter, so it divides opinion, but home-forced chicons kept properly dark are usually milder than shop-bought ones. Forcing types such as Witloof are raised for their long roots, lifted after frost and brought into growth in dark, cool conditions; non-forcing types make larger lettuce-like heads for autumn use. The crop is generally healthy and not difficult, although forcing takes extra work and the roots are easiest to handle when grown in deep, loose soil.

Greenhouse cucumbers are the earliest and highest-yielding cucumbers, capable of producing fruit over a long season and sometimes almost daily in hot weather. They are also one of the more exacting greenhouse crops: seedlings need steady warmth, roots dislike cold wet compost, stems are brittle, and mature plants need careful watering, humid air, feeding, training and stopping. Modern all-female F1 varieties make the crop easier by removing the old job of picking out male flowers and reducing bitterness, while traditional varieties still need male flowers removed. Plants are usually trained vertically on strings, canes or wires, saving space and keeping the fruit clean.

Outdoor cucumbers are fast-growing, frost-tender cucurbits for the warmest part of the season. Modern ridge and outdoor F1 varieties can be smooth, sweet and much less indigestible than older knobbly sorts, while gherkins and apple cucumbers remain useful special cases.

Endive is a cool-season salad plant with more flavour and bitterness than lettuce, though less of lettuce's crispness. It can be eaten raw in mixed salads or cooked, and both curly-leaved frisée types and broader-leaved Batavian or escarole types are useful. Curly endive is usually for late-summer and autumn cutting, while broad-leaved endive is easier to grow for good hearts and is more useful in autumn and winter. The crop needs moisture, humus and some protection from heat or harsh frost; blanching, or choosing self-blanching varieties, gives paler, milder hearts. Small late-summer sowings can provide leaves and hearts into winter, and whole plants lifted in November can give useful fresh salad at Christmas if stored frost-free.

Florence fennel, or bulb fennel, is a sweet, aniseed-flavoured umbellifer grown for the swollen bases of its leaf-stalks. It belongs to the same broad family as carrot, parsnip and celeriac, but is eaten quite differently: sliced raw in salads, cooked gently for a soft creamy flavour, or used in soups and ratatouille. The feathery leaves are also edible, with a mild dill-like flavour. Modern varieties have made it easier to grow by reducing the tendency to bolt before useful bulbs form. Match the variety to its sowing season and keep young plants growing steadily: drought, crowding or root checks can give stemmy plants instead of juicy bulbs. Summer sowings after an early crop are useful for autumn harvesting. Harvest while the bulbs are tender, before they become fibrous, stemmy or frosted.

Garlic is a hardy allium grown from individual cloves, usually planted in autumn for a summer harvest. Home-grown garlic is often more pungent and richly flavoured than bought bulbs, so a little goes a long way in the kitchen. Young plants tolerate very cold winter weather, fit conveniently into the garden after summer crops, and are lifted early enough to be followed by French beans, late brassicas or autumn salads.

Leeks are among the most dependable alliums for a home garden, carrying the harvest from late summer through winter and, with the right varieties, into spring. They quietly gain size while summer crops fade, then provide sweet white shanks and useful green leaves when few fresh vegetables are available. Although closely related to onions, they are generally easier and more tolerant, especially in cool, moist conditions, but they still need a long season, steady moisture, transplanting and some attention to blanching.

Courgettes and marrows are the same general crop at different stages of use: courgettes are picked young, firm and tender, while marrows are allowed to grow larger and can be eaten fresh or stored. Modern courgette varieties are bred to keep producing small fruits, and a well-grown plant in summer warmth can be almost overwhelming, sometimes giving a new courgette every day.

Squashes and pumpkins are vigorous cucurbits grown for fruits that range from tender summer squashes to hard-skinned winter keepers. Summer squashes are picked young, mild and moist, while winter squashes develop firm sweet flesh and hard skins in autumn and can store into winter or spring.

intro: There is something especially exciting about the sight of the first flush of mushrooms breaking through the surface. Mushrooms are fungi rather than vegetables, but they are an obvious choice for a gardener with spare indoor space, because they need no direct sunlight and can be grown when outside beds are quiet. Growing them can be unpredictable: outdoor planting is a gamble, and home-made compost takes considerable preparation. For small quantities, fresh ready-spawned button-mushroom compost is the simplest and most predictable route. Follow the supplier’s instructions for the particular kit, as other mushroom species need different substrates and conditions. Healthy spent compost can be used in the garden after the final crop.

Onions and shallots are among the most useful crops in the kitchen garden, providing fresh bulbs, salads, pickles and winter stores. Spring-planted sets offer a simple start; seed gives a wider choice of colours, sizes and seasonal types. Shallot bulbs usually divide into clusters, while overwintered onions provide earlier harvests.

Oriental leaves are a loose group of quick-growing salad and stir-fry crops, most of them brassicas, which are especially useful after midsummer. They include Chinese cabbage, leaf radish, mibuna, mizuna, mustards, pak choi and shungiku. Their great advantage is speed: many can be cut as baby leaves within a month, while late-summer sowings give cleaner, milder crops with fewer flea beetle holes than spring sowings. They are tender and flavoursome rather than long-storing staples, but they are excellent for filling the salad gap from late summer into autumn, and under cover some leafy types can continue as winter salad leaves.

Parsnips are slow, deep-rooting biennials grown for their long white tap roots, which are at their sweetest after cold weather has turned starches into sugars. They take up the ground for a long season and the seedlings are small and slow to appear, but once established they need little more than clean soil, moisture while young and occasional weeding. Fresh seed is essential, because old seed is the commonest reason for a blank row after a month of waiting. The best roots come from deep, humus-rich, stone-free soil, preferably undug or improved for a previous crop rather than freshly manured.

Peas are one of the great rewards of early summer: a freshly picked pod, eaten straight from the plant, has a sweetness which disappears quickly after picking as the sugars turn to starch. They have long been a staple crop for canning, freezing and drying, but home-grown peas are at their best picked young and cooked or eaten almost immediately.

Potatoes are one of the few crops that can feed a household from a small plot, and they are often the best first crop for newly mulched, newly cleared or rough ground. They are grown from seed potatoes rather than true seed; the planted tuber produces leafy haulm above ground and new tubers below and near the soil surface. Those tubers must be kept covered, because light turns them green and poisonous. First earlies crop quickly and have the finest new-potato flavour; second earlies follow; maincrops give higher yields and better winter storage but need more space and are more exposed to blight.

Rhubarb is grown like a long-lived perennial vegetable, although it is usually cooked and eaten as a fruit. It produces acid, pink-to-red spring stems from large crowns, and the leaves are not eaten. A cold winter helps the plant rest properly; in hot climates or without winter cold, stems may be greener, coarser and less useful. Once established in a damp, compost-rich corner, a crown can crop for many years with little attention beyond feeding, mulching, watering in dry springs and removing flower stems. Stems may be pulled naturally from spring to early summer, or forced in late winter by excluding light, which gives earlier, paler and milder stalks but weakens the plant if done too often.

Spinach is a quick leafy crop which can be available for much of the year with careful planning, but it needs steady moisture and rich soil to avoid bolting. There are summer and winter forms of true spinach, while New Zealand spinach is a separate, frost-tender plant often grown as a summer substitute in hot weather. Perpetual spinach, or spinach beet, is a type of leaf beet rather than true spinach. Choose the appropriate type for the season and pick tender leaves regularly.

Swedes are hardy brassica roots, closely related to turnips but slower growing, sweeter, more substantial and much more frost-resistant. Their flesh is usually orange or yellow, and the leaves arise from a neck above the root rather than directly from the root as in turnips. They are valuable winter vegetables because frost improves their flavour: after cold weather they become sweeter and are good boiled, mashed and seasoned. Swedes need a longer season than turnips, usually about a month more, but they are reliable as a late-sown second crop after early lettuce, carrots, broad beans or other early harvests if given enough room to swell.

Sweet corn is maize picked young, grown for tender, sweet cobs whose sugars begin turning to starch soon after harvest. Home-grown cobs, cooked or eaten very soon after picking, are therefore far superior to shop-bought cobs that have already aged. The crop needs warmth, shelter, good soil and a long enough season, but modern early and supersweet F1 varieties make it far more practical in Britain than older advice sometimes suggests.

Tomato plants are found in the majority of greenhouses during summer, producing a succession of fruit from early summer into autumn. They need constant care: water growing bags or pots regularly in summer and watch for pests and diseases. Home growers can choose flavours and varieties that are rarely sold commercially. Tall or cordon plants are trained with one central stem and their side-shoots removed throughout the season. They need warmth, light, steady root moisture, good ventilation and balanced fertility more than sheer feeding.

Outdoor tomatoes have plenty of flavour to offer, but need a warm, sunny, sheltered site and a variety suited to British summers. Choose plants labelled for outdoor cultivation; in cooler areas, cloches or other protection can make a crop more reliable. Tall cordon tomatoes need staking, side-shooting and stopping near the end of the season so existing fruit can ripen. Bush or determinate tomatoes need less pruning and can be grown under cloches or in containers. Keep low fruit clear of the ground where practical and check for slugs and blight.

Turnips are quick-growing brassica roots, faster and less hardy than swedes. They can be a mild, juicy spring crop if pulled young, a useful catch crop after summer harvests, or a small stored autumn root for winter stews. The roots are generally white-fleshed, with leaves growing directly from the root rather than from a raised neck. Early turnips can come to harvest in 60-80 days, sometimes almost as fast as radishes, while larger autumn roots need longer but should still be eaten before the hardest winter weather. Some varieties also provide useful edible leaves or turnip tops.

Salsify and scorzonera are closely related, old-fashioned root vegetables usually treated together. They are delicacies rather than staples: the roots are long, thin, tender and rather awkward to lift and clean, so usable yields can be modest. Salsify has creamy-coloured roots and is often called vegetable oyster because of its delicate, oyster-like flavour; scorzonera is similar but black-skinned. Both prefer deep, friable soil and direct sowing, and both can stand most winter weather.
